count.idea: Say one number for each object. The last number tells you how many.
count.tip: Do not count the same object twice.

order.idea: Compare place values to put numbers in order.
steps: Compare tens: 2 tens comes before 4 tens.
For 42 and 46, compare ones: 2 comes before 6.
order.tip: Start with the largest place value.

place.idea: A digit’s position tells you its value.
place.tip: A zero holds a place even when there are none of that unit.

tens.tip: Keep tens and ones separate while counting.

partition.idea: You can split the same number in different ways.
steps: Move 100 from the first part to the second.
partition.tip: The parts must add back to the original number.

partitionSmall.idea: Split a number into parts without changing its total.
steps: Now there are 2 tens and 14 ones.
partitionSmall.tip: Check by adding the two parts.

line.idea: A number line shows numbers in order with equal steps.
steps: 30 is three jumps of 10 from zero.
Numbers increase as you move right.
line.tip: Check the size of one step before reading a point.

round.idea: Look at the next digit to decide which nearby ten is closer.
steps: Its ones digit is 7, so round up.
round.tip: Digits 5 to 9 round up; 0 to 4 round down.

roundHundred.idea: Round to the nearest hundred by checking the tens digit.
roundHundred.tip: Rounding gives an estimate, not an exact answer.

even.idea: Even numbers can be put into pairs with none left over.
steps: 8 makes 4 pairs, so it is even.
9 would leave one unpaired, so it is odd.

parity.idea: You can predict whether an answer will be odd or even.
steps: Each odd group has one unpaired object.
Those two leftovers make another pair.
parity.tip: Even + odd is odd; even + even is even.

parityProduct.idea: An even factor makes a product even.
steps: Every group of 4 can be paired.

skip.idea: Skip counting adds the same amount each time.
skip.tip: Check every gap follows the same rule.

add.idea: Adding joins parts to find a total.
add.tip: You can split a number to make 10 first.

subtract.idea: Subtract to find how many are left or how far apart numbers are.

splitAdd.idea: Add tens and ones separately, then join the parts.

splitSubtract.idea: Subtract in parts to make the calculation easier.
splitSubtract.tip: Subtract both the tens and the ones.

compensate.idea: Use a nearby friendly number, then adjust.

doubles.idea: Use a known double to work out a nearby sum.

facts.idea: Addition and subtraction facts belong to the same family.
steps: The parts are 6 and 4; the whole is 10.
Subtract either part to find the other: 10 − 6 = 4.
facts.tip: Subtraction starts with the whole in this fact family.

writtenAdd.idea: Line up place values and regroup when a column totals 10 or more.
writtenAdd.tip: A carried 1 means one unit of the next place.

writtenSubtract.idea: Regroup when there are not enough units to subtract.
writtenSubtract.tip: After exchanging, update both place values.

zeros.idea: Regroup across zero by exchanging a larger unit first.
zeros.tip: An exchange changes the grouping, not the number’s value.

model.idea: Choose an operation that matches what is happening.
model.tip: A drawing can help you decide whether to add or subtract.

twoStep.idea: Solve a multi-step problem one part at a time.
steps: Check that the answer fits the story.
twoStep.tip: Write the result of each step before continuing.

groups.tip: Every group must have the same number.

array.idea: An array arranges equal groups in rows and columns.
steps: Count the objects in one row: 4.
array.tip: Turning the array gives 4 × 3, with the same total.

share.idea: Division can share a total equally.

groupDivide.idea: Division can find how many equal groups fit.
groupDivide.tip: Sharing asks how many in each group; grouping asks how many groups.

mulFacts.idea: Multiplication and division undo each other.
mulFacts.tip: The same three numbers form related facts.

multiply.idea: Split a large multiplication into smaller products.
multiply.tip: Multiply every part, then add the products.

remainders.idea: Sometimes division leaves an amount that cannot make another full group.
steps: There are 3 full groups and 2 left over.
remainders.tip: The remainder must be smaller than the divisor.

remainderContext.idea: What you do with a remainder depends on the problem.
steps: Use one more car: 4 cars altogether.
remainderContext.tip: For full groups only, do not count an incomplete group.

money.idea: Add money amounts using the same units.

change.idea: Change is the amount paid minus the cost.

budget.idea: A budget compares money available with planned spending.
budget.tip: Check all costs before deciding what you can afford.

pattern.idea: A repeating pattern repeats the same unit.
pattern.example: red, blue, red, blue, red, blue
steps: Find the smallest unit: red, blue.
Repeat that unit in the same order.
pattern.tip: A repeating pattern is different from a growing pattern.

fraction.idea: A fraction describes equal parts of a whole.
steps: Split one whole into 4 equal parts.
fraction.tip: The parts must be equal in size.

fractionSet.idea: Find a fraction of a set by sharing it equally.
fractionSet.tip: The denominator tells you how many equal groups.

whole.idea: Unit fractions can join to make one whole.
whole.tip: Keep the whole the same size when comparing parts.

fractionLine.idea: Split each whole-number interval into equal parts.
steps: Split the gap from 0 to 1 into 4 equal steps.

equivalent.idea: Multiply or divide both parts of a fraction by the same number.
steps: The fraction has the same value.
equivalent.tip: Changing only one part changes the fraction’s value.

compareFractions.idea: Use equal denominators to compare fractions.
compareFractions.tip: Use fractions of the same whole.

mixed.idea: An improper fraction can contain whole numbers and a fraction.
steps: 7 quarters leave 3 quarters after that whole.

fractionAdd.idea: With equal denominators, add or subtract the numerators.

commonDenominator.idea: Use a common denominator before adding or subtracting unlike fractions.
commonDenominator.tip: Equivalent fractions keep the original values.

tenths.idea: One tenth is one of ten equal parts of a whole.
steps: Split the whole into 10 equal parts.
tenths.tip: The tenths place is immediately after the decimal point.

hundredths.idea: One hundredth is one of one hundred equal parts.

decimal.idea: Read decimal digits using their place values.

compareDecimals.idea: Compare decimals one place at a time.
steps: Write the numbers with the same number of decimal places.
compareDecimals.tip: More digits does not always mean a larger decimal.

decimalRound.idea: Check the digit immediately after the place you are rounding to.
steps: The next digit is 7, so round up.
decimalRound.tip: Round the original number, not an already rounded version.

decimalAdd.idea: Line up decimal points to add or subtract matching place values.
steps: Add hundredths, then tenths, then ones.
decimalAdd.tip: Adding a trailing zero does not change a decimal’s value.

timesTen.idea: Multiplying by 10 makes each digit worth ten times as much.
timesTen.tip: Multiplying by 100 scales each place by 100.

divideTen.idea: Dividing by 10 makes each digit worth one tenth as much.
divideTen.tip: Dividing by 100 scales each place by one hundredth.

decimalScale.idea: Powers of ten change the value of every digit.
steps: Multiplying by 100 makes 2 ones into 2 hundreds.
3 tenths becomes 3 tens; 5 hundredths becomes 5 ones.
decimalScale.tip: Track place values rather than just adding zeros.

factors.idea: A factor divides a number with no remainder.
steps: List both numbers in each pair.
factors.tip: Stop once the pairs begin to repeat.

multiples.idea: Multiples are the results of multiplying by whole numbers.
steps: Keep adding 6 to find the next multiple.
multiples.tip: Factors divide a number; multiples grow from it.

divisibility.idea: Divisibility rules help you test for factors.
divisibility.tip: For divisibility by 2, check whether the last digit is even.

prime.idea: A prime number has exactly two positive factors: 1 and itself.

square.idea: A square number comes from a whole number multiplied by itself.
steps: Think of a square with 5 rows.

fdp.idea: Fractions, decimals and percentages can show the same amount.

percent.idea: Find a percentage by using easy parts of 100%.
percent.tip: 10% is one tenth and 50% is one half.

discount.idea: A discount is taken off the original price.
discount.tip: The discount amount and the sale price are different.

unitRate.idea: Compare costs for the same quantity.
steps: Divide the total cost by the number of pens.
Compare this with other prices per pen.
unitRate.tip: The cheapest packet may not be the best value per item.

integers.idea: Negative integers are left of zero on a number line.
steps: Numbers increase as you move right.
integers.tip: A negative number with a larger distance from zero is smaller.

integerAdd.idea: Use direction on a number line to add or subtract.
integerAdd.tip: Subtracting a positive number moves you left.

coordinates.idea: A coordinate pair gives horizontal position first, then vertical position.
coordinates.tip: Read the x-coordinate before the y-coordinate.

estimate.idea: Use rounded numbers to check whether an answer is sensible.
steps: Round each number to a friendly value.
The exact answer, 502, is close to 500.
estimate.tip: An estimate helps check an answer; it is not always the final answer.

algorithm.idea: An algorithm is a set of steps followed in order.
steps: Test each step in the stated order.
algorithm.tip: Changing the order can change the answer.

rule.idea: A rule connects each input to its output.
steps: Compare each input with its output.
rule.tip: Check the rule works for every pair.

inverse.idea: Undo an operation using its inverse.
steps: The unknown has 7 added to it.

balance.idea: The equals sign means both sides have the same value.
balance.tip: Equals does not mean “write the answer next”.

unknownFactor.idea: Use division to find a missing factor.
unknownFactor.tip: Use multiplication to check the missing factor.

commutative.idea: You can swap the order when adding or multiplying.
steps: Turn the array to see 7 rows of 4.
commutative.tip: You cannot generally swap numbers in subtraction or division.

associative.idea: When adding or multiplying, you can regroup without changing the order.
steps: Both groupings give the same result.
associative.tip: This regrouping rule does not generally work for subtraction or division.

distributive.idea: Split one factor and multiply both parts.
distributive.tip: Both parts must be multiplied by the other factor.

sequence.idea: Find the change between neighbouring terms.
sequence.tip: Check more than one gap before deciding on a rule.

fractionSequence.idea: Use the same fractional step each time.
fractionSequence.tip: Keep the denominator the same when counting equal parts.

decimalSequence.idea: Decimal sequences follow a repeated change.
decimalSequence.tip: Crossing a whole number does not change the step size.

growth.idea: A table helps connect a stage number with its total.
steps: The total grows by 2 each stage.
Double the stage number, then add 1.
growth.tip: Test a rule against all the known stages.

brackets.idea: Brackets tell you which calculation to do first.

twoUnknown.idea: Use both conditions to find a pair of unknown numbers.
twoUnknown.tip: A pair must satisfy every condition, not just one.

categories.idea: Categorical data sorts answers into named groups.
categories.example: Pets: cat, dog, cat → cat: 2; dog: 1
steps: Place every response in its matching category.
Count how many are in each group.

numerical.idea: Numerical data records a number that counts or measures something.
steps: Ask how many pets each person has.
These are counts, so the data is numerical.
numerical.tip: A number used as a label, such as a shirt number, is not a measurement or count.

question.idea: A useful data question tells you what information to collect.
question.example: Which fruit does our class prefer?
steps: Count the choices in each category.
question.tip: Avoid questions that encourage a particular answer.

tally.idea: Tallies record one mark for each response.
tally.example: 6 responses = one group of 5 tallies + 1 tally
steps: Count groups of five, then leftover marks.
tally.tip: A completed tally group represents five, not four.

table.idea: A frequency table shows how often each value or category occurs.
table.tip: Frequency means the number of times something occurs.

picture.idea: A picture graph uses symbols to show counts.
steps: Read the key: each symbol means 1.
picture.tip: Read the key before counting symbols.

column.idea: A column graph shows counts using bar heights.
steps: Read the category beneath each bar.
Follow its top across to the scale.
Dogs have 6 votes and cats have 4.
column.tip: Check whether the scale counts in ones, twos or another step.

most.idea: Compare frequencies to find the most and least common categories.
steps: 5 is greatest, so red is most common.
2 is smallest, so blue is least common.
most.tip: Two categories can tie for most or least.

difference.idea: Subtract frequencies to find how many more or fewer.
steps: Subtract the smaller from the larger.

evidence.idea: Use the displayed data to check a claim.
evidence.example: Cats: 4; Dogs: 6. “Dogs got more votes.” → true
evidence.tip: Do not make a claim about information that was not collected.

display.idea: Choose a display that makes the data easy to compare.
steps: One column can show the count for each fruit.
A common scale makes counts easy to compare.
display.tip: A different display of the same data must keep the same counts.

key.idea: A picture graph key tells you how much each symbol represents.
steps: Read the key: 4 votes per symbol.
key.tip: A half-symbol would represent 2 votes with this key.

variation.idea: Variation describes how much the data values differ.
steps: Set B is more spread out.
variation.tip: Look at all the values, not just the largest.

shape.idea: Look for clusters, gaps and spread in a distribution.
steps: 9 is far from the main cluster.
shape.tip: Describe what the data shows without guessing why.

ordinal.idea: Ordinal categories have a meaningful order.
steps: They can be put in a meaningful order.
ordinal.tip: Nominal categories, such as colours, have no natural ranking.

validate.idea: Check data for missing, impossible or inconsistent values.
steps: Correct it only if you can verify the intended value.
validate.tip: Do not silently guess or delete unusual values.

mode.idea: The mode is the value that occurs most often.
steps: Count how often each value occurs.
3 occurs twice; the others occur once.
mode.tip: A data set can have more than one mode.

multiMode.idea: Two values can tie for the highest frequency.
multiMode.tip: A mode need not be the greatest numerical value.

lineGraph.idea: A line graph shows how a value changes over time.
steps: Read the time on the horizontal axis.
Read the value on the vertical axis.
Temperature rose by 3°C, then fell by 1°C.
lineGraph.tip: Use the scale to measure change; do not rely only on the slope’s appearance.

continuous.idea: Continuous data comes from measuring and can include values between whole numbers.
steps: A length can fall between these values.
continuous.tip: The number of pencils is a count: discrete data.

range.idea: Range measures the gap between the greatest and smallest values.
range.tip: Range uses the extremes, not the most frequent value.

compareData.idea: Compare groups using the same measures and scales.
steps: Group B has higher values overall.
Describe both typical values and spread.
compareData.tip: A larger sample can have more responses without a larger typical value.

misleading.idea: Graph scales can make small differences look large.
steps: Read where the vertical scale starts.
A scale starting at 97 exaggerates the visual gap.
misleading.tip: Check labels, units, scale intervals and any breaks in the axis.

units.idea: Choose a unit that suits what you are measuring.
units.example: A pencil: centimetres. A road: kilometres.
steps: Think about the size of the object.
Choose a unit that gives a useful measurement.
units.tip: Use litres for capacity and grams or kilograms for mass.

turn.idea: A turn describes how far something rotates.
steps: A full turn returns to the starting direction.
A half turn faces the opposite direction.
A quarter turn is halfway to a half turn.
turn.tip: Check whether the turn is clockwise or anticlockwise.

areaPerimeter.idea: Area measures the surface; perimeter measures the boundary.
areaPerimeter.example: 3 × 4 rectangle: area 12 square units; perimeter 14 units
areaPerimeter.tip: Shapes with the same area can have different perimeters.

area.idea: A rectangle’s area is the number of unit squares covering it.
area.example: 4 rows of 6 squares → area 24 square units
area.tip: Area uses square units, such as cm².

composite.idea: Split a composite shape into rectangles without gaps or overlaps.
composite.example: Rectangle areas 12 cm² and 8 cm² → total 20 cm²
steps: Choose a split that makes rectangles.
composite.tip: Do not count an overlapping area twice.

protractor.idea: Place a protractor carefully before reading or drawing an angle.
protractor.example: To draw 60°, mark 60 on the correct scale
steps: Put the centre on the vertex.
Line up zero with the starting ray.
Mark 60° and draw a ray through the mark.
protractor.tip: Use the scale that starts at zero on your starting ray.

angleEstimate.idea: Compare an angle with familiar benchmarks.
angleEstimate.example: An angle smaller than 90° is acute
steps: Use a right angle as a benchmark.
An angle near half a right angle is about 45°.
Estimate first, then measure if needed.
angleEstimate.tip: An obtuse angle is greater than 90° and less than 180°.

metric.tip: Smaller units need a larger numerical count for the same amount.

time.idea: Break a time interval into manageable jumps.

timetable.idea: Use departure and arrival times to check a journey.
timetable.tip: Leave enough time between connecting services.

anglesPoint.idea: Angles around a point add to 360°.
anglesPoint.tip: Angles on a straight line add to 180° instead.

design.idea: A measurement design must meet every given condition.
design.example: A 6 m by 4 m garden needs 20 m of edging
steps: Identify what is needed: the boundary.
Check the available edging is at least 20 m.
design.tip: List the conditions and units before choosing a design.

placeLarge.idea: Each place is ten times the value of the place to its right.
steps: There are no tens and 6 ones.
placeLarge.tip: The zero keeps the tens place.

partitionLarge.idea: Rename a number by exchanging place-value units.
partitionLarge.tip: Add the parts to check the total.

decimalLine.idea: Read the interval between labelled points before locating a decimal.
decimalLine.tip: Equal distances on the line represent equal differences.

friendlyMultiply.idea: Use a nearby easy multiplication, then adjust.
steps: Nine groups need one fewer group.
friendlyMultiply.tip: Subtract one whole group, not just one.

sixes.idea: Double a known three-times fact to find a six-times fact.
steps: Six groups are twice as many as three.
sixes.tip: Doubling the number of groups doubles the total.

sevens.idea: Split seven groups into five groups and two groups.
sevens.tip: Keep the group size the same when splitting.

nestedUnknown.idea: Undo the outside operation first, then the operation inside the brackets.
nestedUnknown.tip: Keep the bracketed part together while undoing the outside operation.

eitherSide.idea: An equation works the same way with the unknown on either side.
eitherSide.tip: The equals sign means both sides have the same value.

pairsUnknown.idea: An equation with two unknowns can have several pairs of solutions.
steps: Choose a value for a, such as 3.
pairsUnknown.tip: Follow any limits on which numbers are allowed.

lists.idea: A list records each response before you organise the data.
steps: Keep both cat responses: they came from different people.
lists.tip: Repeated answers are still separate pieces of data.

doubleHalve.idea: Doubling makes two equal copies. Halving splits a total into two equal parts.
steps: Halve 16: share it into 2 equal groups.
Each group has 8, so halving undoes doubling.
doubleHalve.tip: Check the direction of the rule: double or halve.
